scenes.sub: An array quietly turns into a pointer, and forgets its size.
scenes.say: Array decay. An array quietly turns into a pointer to its first element, and in the process, it forgets its own size. Let's watch it happen.

scenes.head: The array becomes a pointer

panels.code:
int arr[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};

int* p = arr;  // same as &arr[0]

sizeof(arr);   // 16: whole array
sizeof(p);     // 8: just a pointer

scenes.say: Here's an array of four ints, sixteen bytes side by side. Now, int star p equals arr. We never wrote ampersand, but the array silently converts to a pointer to its first element. That's array decay. Ask sizeof of the array, and you get sixteen, the whole thing. Ask sizeof of p, and you get eight on a sixty four bit machine. The pointer knows where the array starts, but it forgets the length.

scenes.head: Where it bites: function parameters
scenes.say: Decay bites hardest with functions. You can't pass a plain array by value. Even if you write the parameter with brackets and a size, the four is ignored, and the parameter is really an int pointer. The array decays at the call. So inside print, sizeof gives the pointer size. The program prints sixteen, then eight. That's why C style functions always take the length as a separate argument.

scenes.head: When it doesn't decay, and the modern fix

panels.code:
int arr[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};

auto  q = &arr;              // int(*)[4]: size kept
auto& r = arr;               // int(&)[4]: no decay

template <std::size_t N>
void show(int (&a)[N]);      // N deduced as 4

void show(std::span<int> s); // C++20: pointer + length
std::array<int, 4> safe{};   // never decays

scenes.say: Decay doesn't happen everywhere. sizeof and the ampersand operator see the real array, so address of arr is a pointer to an array of four. Binding a reference also keeps the full type. That lets a template take the array by reference and deduce N as four. In modern C plus plus, use s t d colon colon array, which never decays, or pass a s t d colon colon span, which carries the pointer and length together. Interview trap: arrays are not pointers. They just convert to one.

lines: Array decay: an array converts to a pointer to its first element.
The size is lost: sizeof gives pointer size, functions can't know the length.
No decay with sizeof, &, or references. Prefer std::array or std::span.
scenes.say: Array decay is the implicit conversion of an array to a pointer to its first element. The size is lost, so a function receiving it can't know the length. It doesn't happen with sizeof, ampersand, or references. Prefer s t d colon colon array or span.
